purpose: Machine-readable reference for the Mwezi Quarter seafront. tools/blender/create_seafront_kit_v1.py reads this file and builds the assets from it; docs/art/references/comorian-seafront-reference-v1.md documents every field and its source. Change a value here and regenerate -- never hand-edit the generated assets.

provenance.photograph_note: No photographs were viewable by the authoring environment. Version 2.0.0 replaces the earlier photo-dependent placeholders with values taken from written descriptions of the two historic quarters of Moroni's medina, Badjanani and Mtsangani. Fields are labelled `description-sourced` where a written account states them, `assumed` where they are an authoring choice, and `unresolved` where no consulted description settles them.
provenance.creative_property: README section 67 and the 2026-09-17 human decision keep the in-game place renamed and fictional. This spec captures architectural morphology, not identity: no real building, real place name or religious function is reproduced. The hall is a secular civic ruin.
provenance.religious_omissions: Descriptions of the real building name features that are religious identifiers: a green dome on the minaret, Quranic verses carved into the walls, and a mihrab. These are deliberately NOT modelled. README section 67 and the 2026-09-17 decision make the in-game hall a secular civic ruin, so the kit takes only the secular morphology -- dark volcanic base, white rendered walls, arcades on slender columns, flat roof, slender corner tower -- and omits every religious marker.

site.description: A stone quarter meeting the sea on a volcanic coast. The quarter's civic hall stands at the water's edge on a raised platform; a quay runs along the harbour front; black lava rock forms the shoreline where there is no built edge; the medina's alleys run back from the water.
site.notes: Wikivoyage: the mosque 'sits on the harbor adjacent to a shipyard and the medina'; the medina is 'winding alleys between ancient buildings'. Wikipedia: Moroni has 'a rocky volcanic coastline, mostly without beaches'.

sea.notes: Indian Ocean off a reef coast reads deep blue-green offshore and turquoise over shallow coral. Level sits below the quay coping so the wall has visible freeboard. Swell wavelength is a long ocean swell, not a wind chop: at 140 m across a 36-column grid the sample spacing is ~3.9 m, so a short wavelength aliases rather than reads.

shoreline.notes: Wikivoyage describes the island's first impression as a 'volcanic island of harsh black rock'; Wikipedia confirms a rocky volcanic coastline mostly without beaches. Near-black basalt is the single strongest contrast against the lime-washed stone.

beach_pocket.notes: Mtsangani's beaches are described as among the finest in Moroni, which qualifies the island-wide 'mostly without beaches'. The shore is therefore lava rock interrupted by a sand pocket, not lava alone. Built as its own asset rather than folded into the lava tile: at 18 m it is wider than most of the 22 m lava run, so mixing them would make every shore tile part beach. The level lays lava runs and interrupts them with one pocket.

quay.notes: Wikipedia gives Moroni's port an '80 metres quay with a draught of 3.5 metres'. The 80 m is the real-world reference; the asset is a 12 m tile so the level can lay any run length.

civic_hall.description: The quarter's landmark at the water's edge: a low whitewashed coral-stone hall with an arcaded seaward front, a flat roof behind a parapet, and a square tower at one corner. Secular civic ruin in fiction.
civic_hall.notes: Described as sitting above the shallow port overlooking the ocean, with 'roches volcaniques sombres a sa base' under 'murs d'un blanc immacule', 'arcs elegants', 'colonnes raffinees', a polished stone floor and local timber ceilings, and a slender tower visible across the city and added as a later campaign. The dark base under white walls is a correction: the first version stood the hall on a pale coral platform. Dimensions, bay count and tower height remain unresolved -- no consulted description gives a measurement -- and the dating is itself contested (see the reference document). Two further corrections in 2.0.0: platform_height_m was deleted so volcanic_base_height_m is the single source for the plinth (the plinth IS the dark volcanic base, not a pale platform with a base on top), and arcade_pier_width_m dropped 0.72 -> 0.52 because 0.72 m square piers on a 2.4 m span read as piers, not as the 'colonnes raffinees' the description names.
civic_hall.wall_finish: immaculate white lime render above a dark volcanic rock base

materials.notes: Sources name coral stone, whitewashed walls and carved wooden doors against dark volcanic rock. Two values correct earlier assumptions. First: where the plaster has collapsed the stone beneath is described as 'noires comme de l'encre' -- ink-black basalt, not pale coral rag, so plaster_loss_core is near-black. Second: the medina's woodwork is 'd'un bois fendillé, blanchi par l'age et le climat' -- split and bleached by age and climate -- so weathered_timber is a pale grey-brown rather than the dark hardwood first used. The overall palette is explicitly 'un melange de blancheur et de noirceur'. carved_hardwood was removed in 2.0.0 rather than left beside its replacement: two timber values in one palette is exactly how a corrected colour quietly comes back.

vegetation.notes: Coconut palms are standard on this coast. Count is an authoring choice for skyline break-up, not a sourced figure.

medina.description: Moroni's medina is formed by two historic quarters: Mtsangani to the north and Badjanani to the south, the latter holding the principal mosque and the main market.
medina.wall_mix: basalt, crushed coral and sea sand
medina.notes: Lettres-ocean: buildings 'ont generalement un, deux ou trois etages', rarely four; walls are 'un melange de basalte, de corail broye et de sable de mer'; passages are sometimes 'aussi minces que des failles rocheuses'; two main commercial streets link the upper and lower town; roofs are flat. Alley widths are the authoring reading of 'as narrow as rock fissures' against a walkable minimum.
